title: Why didn't you think well?
hook: when you heard the slander, why didn't believers think good of their own (24:12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Verse of Light, and your line was light upon light. Which lamp did you notice last night? Day four hundred ninety-three.

An army is on its way home through the desert. At one stop, a young woman steps away from camp, and on the way back finds her necklace is missing. She goes back to look for it. When she returns, the camp is gone. Her litter was loaded onto the camel without anyone noticing she wasn't inside. She waits. A man who traveled behind the army finds her, lets her ride, and leads the camel back on foot. They arrive together, in daylight. And within hours, people are talking. The woman is 'A'isha, the Prophet's wife. Today, the rumor.

Bukhari preserves 'A'isha's own long account. The rumor spread through Medina for about a month. She fell ill and didn't know what was being said until a woman told her. She wept for two nights. Then verses of Surah An-Nur came down, declaring her innocent. And look at the first question those verses ask. Not, why did the slanderers lie? But this, in Pickthall's words: "Why did not the believers, men and women, when ye heard it, think good of their own folk, and say: It is a manifest untruth?" The question is aimed at the listeners. The ordinary people who heard it and passed it on, or just let it sit in their heads. A few verses later the surah describes how it happened: you took it up with your tongues, and spoke with your mouths of what you had no knowledge of, and counted it a small thing, when with God it was great. That's how a rumor travels: it seems small. The word this day carries is husn al-zann: thinking well. Zann is an assumption, a guess about someone you can't fully see. Husn is goodness. So husn al-zann is choosing the good guess. And a hadith in Bukhari gives the other side: beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most false of talk. The surah doesn't ask people to be naive. It asks them to begin from good faith, especially about their own, and to say plainly when something is unproven. Think well first. The facts can come after.
screen: `'A'ISHA'S OWN ACCOUNT.` · `THE QUESTION IS FOR THE LISTENERS.` · `IT SEEMED SMALL; IT WAS GREAT.` · `HUSN AL-ZANN: CHOOSE THE GOOD GUESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: assume the best of someone. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one person whose behavior lately has bothered you. A late reply, a cold tone, a decision you didn't understand. Now come up with three generous explanations for it. Not excuses, just possibilities you can't rule out. Hold the kindest one for a while. If you pray, you can ask to think well of them. The bell holds the time.
Husn al-zann. Thinking well: choosing the good assumption about someone when you don't know the whole story. Today's word.
Your line: think well first. Today, when a piece of gossip reaches you, let it stop with you. Day four hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often cite 24:12 and the story of the slander, the ifk, when teaching about rumor and gossip, and encourage husn al-zann, thinking well of others, as an everyday habit.

match.prompt: inside the story — tap the pairs.

myth: 24:12 is aimed mainly at the people who invented the rumor
its question is aimed at the listeners: why didn't you think well and call it untrue?
'A'isha's own account of the rumor is preserved in Bukhari
she tells of the lost necklace, her illness, and the verses that cleared her.
the surah asks believers to believe whatever they hear about others
it asks them to think well first, and to call an unproven charge untrue.

fork.setup: you hear that a woman of good character arrived in camp with a man not her husband, after being left behind. people are already talking. what does the surah say you should have done?
options: ask around to find out more.
think well of her, and say: this is plainly untrue.
stay quiet but keep it in mind.
fork.reveal: think good of your own folk and call it an obvious untruth. the verses ask why the listeners didn't.

original.note: Arabic: husn al-zann, thinking well; zann is an assumption, husn is goodness.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't spread rumors.
what it means: the first duty falls on the listener: begin from a good assumption about others, and call an unproven charge untrue.
what a scholar hears: 24:11–20 respond to the hadith al-ifk (Bukhari 4750), traditionally placed after the campaign of Banu al-Mustaliq; zann can mean both conjecture and assumption.

sources.quoted: Why did not the believers, men and women, when ye heard it, think good of their own folk, and say: It is a manifest untruth?

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4750 ('A'isha's account of the slander)

notes: Pickthall wording of 24:12 quoted from memory; please confirm exactly.

The story follows 'A'isha's account in Bukhari 4750 as Sunni tradition preserves it; the man is Safwan ibn al-Mu'attal (not named in the script). Shia commentators accept that 24:11 concerns a slander but some narrations link it to a different occasion; a Keeper may want a sentence on this.
'About a month' and 'two nights' of weeping follow the hadith; confirm details.
Bukhari numbers 4750 and 6066 cited from memory; confirm.
Editor review 2026-10-01: one line no longer tells the listener what passing on a rumor feels like; otherwise checked against Bukhari 4750 and left as is.
